Self-Serve vs Managed Desk vs Agency: Who Runs Your Media?

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 16 February 2026 · 7-minute read · Distribution

Self-serve suits small budgets in categories the platforms welcome, provided someone refuses the defaults, which are designed around the platform's revenue. A flat-fee managed desk suits budgets past the fee floor, restricted categories and channels beyond the self-serve platforms. An agency suits large, multi-channel spend where buying power and planning matter more than fee structure. Whatever you choose, the ad accounts, conversion tracking, pixel history and analytics stay in your company's name.

Every media platform now offers a self-serve interface. Anyone with a card can open an account, upload creative, choose an audience and spend money within an hour. That raises a fair question: why pay anyone to do it for you?

The answer depends on three things: how much you spend, how much time you have, and whether the platforms will take your money at all.

Option one: run it yourself

Self-serve works when the budget is small, the product is in a category the platforms welcome, and someone on the team has the time to learn the interface and check the numbers daily.

The advantages are obvious. No fee. Full control. Direct access to the data. The disadvantages are less visible. The interface is designed by the platform to maximise the platform's revenue, and its defaults (broad audiences, automated placements and optimisation toward cheap events) serve that purpose. A self-serve buyer who accepts the defaults is spending efficiently for the platform.

The defaults are documented. Google's auto-apply recommendations, once switched on, can add broad match keywords, add audiences, turn on Display Expansion and change CPA and ROAS targets without a person approving each change. Google's own page says auto-apply does not raise budgets. Until October 2026, Search campaigns with Display Expansion used unspent search budget on the Display Network with a backend 50% allocation that advertisers could neither see nor change; Google has since added a visible priority setting and will move these campaigns to channel prioritisation automatically from February 2027. A self-serve buyer has to know these settings exist to refuse them.

Self-serve also stops at the platform's edge. Programmatic buying at any scale, creator programmes, affiliate networks and cross-channel measurement are not self-serve products. And if the category is restricted, the self-serve interface is where you will find that out, usually after building an account you cannot use. Our explainer on restricted categories covers how platforms review them.

Option two: a managed desk at a flat fee

A desk is a small team that runs the accounts on your behalf, in your name, for a fixed monthly fee per account. It sets inventory standards, manages verification, refreshes creative, optimises toward the outcome you care about, and reports the numbers that matter: real cost per impression after verification, rejection rate, cost per outcome your own tracking confirms.

The fee does not change with spend, which means the desk earns nothing extra by spending more. That is the point. It also means there is a floor: below a certain monthly budget, the fee is a large share of the total and the arrangement stops making sense.

Where the floor sits is a unit-economics question: our piece on demand generation economics covers how to set a budget from cost per qualified opportunity and payback. A desk is right when the budget is past the floor, the channels include programmatic or anything beyond the self-serve platforms, and you want the accounts, the data and the history to stay yours. Our guide to pricing architecture for services firms covers how fixed-fee models are structured more generally.

Option three: an agency on a percentage

A traditional agency arrangement bundles planning, buying, creative and reporting for a percentage of media spend, sometimes with the agency fronting the spend and billing you afterwards.

It scales well for large budgets and complex, multi-channel plans. It also creates the incentive problem discussed in our piece on percent-of-spend fees: the agency earns more when you spend more, and an agency that fronts spend controls the account history and platform relationships that should belong to you. The ANA's 2022 compensation study found 19% of marketers still paid commissions for media planning and buying, nearly three times the rate for agency services overall.

The largest advertisers have been moving the other way. The ANA's 2023 in-house agency survey found 82% of members had in-house agencies, up from 42% in 2008, and 54% of those handled some media planning or buying. Owning and protecting first-party data was a key driver. Those who had not brought media in-house most often called it "too complex", which is the gap a desk or a specialist partner fills.

A partner who insists on holding your ad accounts is asking to own the part of your business that is hardest to rebuild.

How to decide

Spending under a few thousand a month, in a welcome category, with time to learn: run it yourself, and refuse the defaults. Review auto-apply settings, network settings and audience expansion before launch, and check them monthly.

Spending past the floor, or in a category the platforms review, or needing programmatic and other channels beyond self-serve: a managed desk on a flat fee, with the accounts in your name.

Spending at a scale where buying power and multi-channel planning matter more than fee structure: an agency, with a contract that keeps the accounts yours and states the fee in dollars rather than as a percentage. Our guide to running a marketing RFP covers how to compare proposals.

The one thing to keep in every case

Whoever runs the media, the ad accounts, the conversion tracking, the pixel history and the analytics should be in your company's name.

This is a matter of platform mechanics, not only principle. Google Ads' access documentation says that if a manager account has ownership of your account, its admins can edit user access, managers and product links within your account. It also recommends having more than one admin, because access to tags can be lost if the only admin becomes unavailable. The company should hold admin rights itself and grant partners standard access. Our piece on how marketing tracking works lists the rest of the measurement layer to keep.

lowob takeaways

  • Refuse the defaults. Self-serve settings are designed around the platform's revenue; know which ones apply changes without approval.
  • A flat fee removes the spend incentive. Below a certain budget, though, the fee is too large a share.
  • Agencies suit scale, with contracts that keep accounts yours. State the fee in dollars.
  • Hold admin rights yourself. Ad accounts, conversion tracking, pixel history and analytics in the company's name.

Common questions

Should I run my own ads or hire an agency?

Run it yourself if you spend under a few thousand a month in a welcome category and have time to learn. Use a flat-fee managed desk past that floor or in restricted categories, and an agency when buying power and multi-channel planning matter most.

What is a managed media desk?

A small team that runs ad accounts in your name for a fixed monthly fee per account, setting inventory standards, managing verification, refreshing creative and reporting costs confirmed by your own tracking.

Should I turn on Google Ads auto-apply recommendations?

Only for recommendation types you have reviewed. Once on, auto-apply can add broad match keywords, audiences and Display Expansion and change bid targets without anyone approving each change.

Who should own the ad accounts when working with an agency?

Your company. Hold admin rights and give the partner standard access. If a partner's manager account owns your account, its admins can change who has access to it.
